prompts.question: Outline ONE way that traditional owners can be involved in a large-scale mining operation.
markerNotes: Give one specific way traditional owners take part, placed at a stage of the operation such as planning, operation or rehabilitation.
Say what the traditional owners do in that role. Stating that they are important or have a say does not outline a way of being involved.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the history or culture of the land rather than how traditional owners take part in the mine.
Giving a general statement that traditional owners are important to the mine, with no role named.
keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples

2 marks: Outlines a way traditional owners can be involved in a large-scale mining operation

sampleAnswers.answer: In the planning phase of a mining operation, traditional owners can be involved in surveying the proposed mining operation to assess and minimise the impact of mining on culture and heritage.

sampleAnswers.answer: Traditional owners can have a say about the mine.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. Having a say names no particular role, so it does not outline a way of being involved. Naming one stage, such as planning, and what the owners do there would meet the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Write a valid method for an investigation to address the students’ aim.
markerNotes: A valid method names the variable being compared (the area), the variable measured (the weight of recyclable waste), and the controlled variables, and says how the data is gathered.
Give the steps in order and repeat them, so someone else could carry the method out and the areas can be compared.
commonStudentErrors: Listing collection steps without naming any variable.
Measuring only one area, so the method cannot compare areas to address the aim.
Writing a result or a conclusion instead of the method.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Constructs a valid method to address the students’ aim; Method includes gathering data, a dependent, an independent and a controlled variable
3 marks: Constructs a sound, logical method to address the students’ aim; Method includes reference to more than ONE variable
2 marks: Outlines a way that waste can be collected, sorted or measured
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
1. Bins are to be collected from the office, outdoor seating and classrooms after lunch each day.
2. The contents of each bin to be tipped on to separate plastic sheets and sorted into recyclable and non-recyclable waste.
3. Each category of waste to be weighed and recorded in a table.
4. Steps 1–3 to be repeated for 3 weeks.
5. Averages to be collected for each area and compared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by constructing a valid, numbered method that gathers data, compares areas, weighs each category of waste and repeats the steps for 3 weeks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Collect the waste from each bin and sort it into recyclable and non-recyclable piles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining a way waste can be collected and sorted. It names no variables and no repeats, so it does not reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Look at what goes into the bins.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It gives no way to collect, sort or measure the waste.

prompts.question: Describe ONE method of determining the age of a rock layer, other than absolute (radiometric) dating.
markerNotes: Choose a relative method, not radiometric dating, and say how it places the layer in time, through its position or its fossils.
The description needs the rule or the step, for example the order of the layers, not only the name of the method.
commonStudentErrors: Naming radiometric or carbon dating, which the question rules out.
Naming superposition or index fossils without saying how they give the age of the layer.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes ONE suitable method of dating a rock layer other than absolute dating
2 marks: Outlines a suitable method of dating a rock layer
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: An index fossil is associated with a known, narrow time interval. If an index fossil is found in the rock layer, the age of the rock layer is the same as the index fossil.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing a relative dating method, an index fossil, and explaining how finding it in a layer gives the layer its age.

sampleAnswers.answer: Superposition can be used to date rock layers, with older layers at the bottom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining a suitable relative method. It names the rule but does not explain how it gives the age of this layer, which the 3-mark row requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rocks can be dated by looking at them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names no method, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Contrast TWO effects of human activity and cyanobacteria on the atmosphere.
markerNotes: Give two differences, each setting one human effect against the matching cyanobacterial effect on the same gas or process.
Name the gas in each contrast, such as oxygen or carbon dioxide, and whether it is added to or removed from the atmosphere.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the effects of humans and cyanobacteria separately with no contrast.
Writing about cyanobacteria's effect on rocks, such as banded iron formations, rather than on the atmosphere.
Stating that both change the atmosphere without saying which gas or in which direction.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Provides TWO differences between human and cyanobacterial effects on the atmosphere
2 marks: Provides differences between human and cyanobacterial effects on the atmosphere OR provides ONE related difference
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Respiration is a human activity which removes O2 from the atmosphere and replaces it with CO2 whereas cyanobacteria have the opposite effect due to photosynthesis; removing CO2 and replacing it with O2. Human industrial activities have added CO2 to the atmosphere over centuries while cyanobacteria have been removing CO2 from the atmosphere over billions of years.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by giving two differences between human and cyanobacterial effects on the atmosphere, each naming the gas and the direction of change.

sampleAnswers.answer: Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, unlike cyanobacteria, which release oxygen.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by giving one related difference between human and cyanobacterial effects on the atmosphere. A second difference would meet the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cyanobacteria and humans both change the atmosphere.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information. It names a shared effect but no difference, so it does not contrast anything.

prompts.question: Explain why the focus of some earthquakes is deeper than others.
markerNotes: Link the depth of the focus to the plate boundary and to what happens to the crust there, such as subduction.
Use the term focus (hypocentre) correctly and say whether the focus is shallow or deep in the case given.
commonStudentErrors: Confusing the focus with the epicentre, which is the point on the surface above the focus.
Saying deeper earthquakes are stronger, which is a claim about intensity, not focus depth.
Describing focus depths without explaining why they vary between earthquakes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains why an earthquake focus varies in depth
2 marks: Explains why an earthquake focus is either shallow or deep OR Describes a cause of both shallow and deep earthquakes
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: At a subduction zone, near the plate boundary the earthquakes are shallow as the crust is close to the surface. As the crust is subducted deeper below the surface, the pressure consequently builds up deeper below the surface, leading to a deeper earthquake focus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining why the focus varies in depth at subduction zones, linking shallow and deep foci to how far the crust is subducted.

sampleAnswers.answer: Deep earthquakes occur where the subducting plate sinks further into the mantle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining why a focus is deep. It does not explain why other foci are shallow, so the answer does not reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Earthquakes happen when rock breaks along a fault.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Siberian Traps were formed by massive outpouring of lava over millions of years. These eruptions produced huge amounts of SO2 and CO2. prompts.question:
Evaluate the effectiveness of planting native trees in solving problems studied in the Earth and Environmental Science course. Support your answer with TWO specific, unrelated examples.
Examples may include:
• natural disasters
• resource management problems
• climate related problems
• other environmental problems.
markerNotes: Use two unrelated problems, and for each explain the mechanism by which native trees address it, then judge how effective planting is for that problem.
The judgement must be stated and supported by the examples, with at least one limit, such as the years trees need to store carbon or their need for water.
A strong answer names the problem first and then links the tree process to it, instead of listing benefits of trees in general.
commonStudentErrors: Discussing one problem only, so the answer cannot reach the top rows.
Listing benefits of trees without naming an environmental problem they solve.
Giving a judgement, such as planting is effective, with no criteria or reason.
Using a problem that is not from the course, such as a general pollution issue, to support the answer.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding of TWO problems to explain how planting native trees can solve identified problems; Makes clearly supported judgements based on criteria
6-7 marks: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding of TWO problems to explain how planting native trees can solve identified problems; Makes a supported judgement based on criteria
4-5 marks: Demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding of how planting trees can solve problem(s); Makes a judgement
2-3 marks: Demonstrates basic knowledge and understanding of the benefits of trees OR Outlines relevant environmental problem(s)
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Anthropogenic climate change is caused by activities such as burning coal to generate electricity, which introduces excess CO2 into the atmosphere. CO2 traps the Sun’s heat causing global warming. As native trees grow, they photosynthesise, capturing CO2 from the atmosphere and locking the carbon in their wood. Trees draw water from the soil by transpiration, which draws heat from surrounding air to evaporate water from the tree’s leaves. This cools the air around the tree, reducing local warmer temperatures. Mines produce large quantities of tailings, waste material which can escape causing dust pollution in the air and contaminating waterways. Tailings are stored in dams. During mine reclamation the tailings dam is covered in topsoil and trees are planted over the dam. Tree roots stabilise the soil, which contains the tailings by preventing erosion. Choosing native trees also provides habitat. Planting deep rooted native trees is very effective in combating climate change because they capture CO2, act as a carbon sink and lower local temperatures. Trees successfully contain mine tailings protecting the surrounding environment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 8-mark row by explaining how native trees address two unrelated problems, climate change through carbon capture and mine tailings through root stabilisation, and by making a supported judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Planting native trees is effective against climate change. Trees take in CO₂ during photosynthesis and store carbon in their wood, which reduces the CO₂ in the atmosphere. Transpiration also draws heat from the surrounding air, which cools the local area. However, trees take many years to store a large amount of carbon, so planting is a slow response to rising temperatures.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4–5 row by showing sound knowledge of how planting trees solves one problem, and by making a judgement. Only one problem is used, so the answer does not reach the 6–7 row; a second unrelated problem with a supported judgement would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Native trees are good for the environment because they take in carbon dioxide and provide habitat for animals.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2–3 row by showing basic knowledge of the benefits of trees. No environmental problem is named and no judgement is made, so it does not reach the 4–5 row.

prompts.question: Assess the effect of TWO human activities on the sustainability of water resources.
markerNotes: Name two human activities and, for each, the effect on the water resource and how that effect limits its future use, which is the sustainability link.
Add a judgement of how sustainable each activity is, with a reason, to move above description.

4 marks: Assesses the effect of TWO human activities on water resources; Implies a link to sustainability
3 marks: Explains the effect of ONE human activity on a water resource; Implies a link to sustainability; Provides or implies a judgement OR Describes the effect of TWO human activities on water resources; Provides or implies a judgement

1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Sustainability involves meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs. Pollution is a human activity that adds litter and chemicals to waterways, such as microplastics, agricultural run-off or oils from transport. This negatively impacts the sustainability of water as a resource as it blocks waterways and reduces water quality for aquatic organisms. The reduction in water quality makes the water unsafe for humans to use in the future. Off-creek water storage dams, where water is taken from rivers during high-flow with good quality and stored for future use is a very sustainable practice. This ensures water-flow and quality in rivers during times of drought, whilst meeting the needs of a community for access to water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by assessing the effect of two human activities, pollution and off-creek water storage, and clearly linking each to the sustainability of water.

sampleAnswers.answer: Agricultural run-off carries fertilisers and chemicals into rivers. This reduces water quality for aquatic organisms and people, so the practice is not sustainable because future users cannot rely on clean water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the effect of one human activity on a water resource, implying a link to sustainability and giving a judgement. A second activity with its own effect and judgement would reach the 4–5 rows.

sampleAnswers.answer: Water is an important resource that many people depend on.
